title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project management. The key reason someone would switch is to take advantage of Plane's self-hosted option and cost savings.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Plane is free to use when self-hosted, while Jira has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Plane allows for full data ownership since it can be self-hosted, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, while Jira offers a more straightforward setup process.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large, complex projects, while Plane may require more configuration to scale.
* Integration difference: Jira has a more extensive library of integrations with third-party tools, while Plane has a more limited but growing set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Jira
* Extensive library of integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable and suitable for large, complex projects
* User-friendly interface
* Robust customer support
* Wide range of features for project management
### Plane
* Free to use when self-hosted
* Full data ownership
* Customizable and flexible
* Growing community of users and developers
* Limited costs for small to medium-sized teams

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large teams or complex projects that require a wide range of features and integrations. Its scalability and robust customer support make it a reliable option for teams that need a comprehensive project management solution. On the other hand, Plane is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or projects that require a high degree of customization and data ownership. Its self-hosted option and free cost make it an attractive choice for teams on a budget.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use the Plane import tool to migrate your data, or manually import it if necessary.
3. Configure your Plane instance to match your Jira setup, including workflows and permissions.
4. Test your Plane instance to ensure all features and integrations are working as expected.
5. Train your team on the new Plane interface and features.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's self-hosting requirements can be demanding, and teams may need to invest in additional hardware or expertise to host it effectively. However, for teams that value data ownership and cost savings, Plane is a viable alternative to Jira, and we recommend considering it for small to medium-sized projects or teams that do not require the full range of Jira's features.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need extensive integrations
* Projects with simple workflows that do not require Jira's advanced features
* Teams on a tight budget that cannot afford Jira's per-user fees
* Projects that require full data ownership and control
* Development teams that value customization and flexibility

## FAQ
### Is Plane free to use?
Yes, Plane is free to use when self-hosted, but teams may need to invest in hardware or expertise to host it effectively.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using its import tool.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane may not be suitable for large teams or complex projects that require a wide range of features and integrations.
### Does Plane have a user-friendly interface?
Plane's interface is customizable and flexible, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and use effectively.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet, Plane is still developing and may lack some of the features and polish of Jira.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: WeKan is a free, self-hosted alternative to Trello. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are cloud storage solutions that enable individuals and teams to store, share, and collaborate on files. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a proprietary cloud storage solution to a self-hosted or open-source alternative, with the core use case being secure and flexible file management. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Nextcloud can be more scalable than Dropbox, especially for large teams or enterprises with self-hosting capabilities.
* Integration with onlyOffice: Nextcloud has native integration with onlyOffice for document editing, whereas Dropbox relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $1998-$3316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of third-party integrations
* Robust security features
* Cross-platform compatibility
* Limited control over data and customization options
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosting capabilities for full data control
* High scalability and flexibility
* Open-source and extensible
* Integration with onlyOffice for document editing
* Steeper learning curve and technical requirements for setup and maintenance

## When to Choose Each
When to choose Dropbox: Dropbox is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who prioritize ease of use and don't require advanced customization or control over their data. It's ideal for teams that already use a range of third-party tools and services that integrate with Dropbox.
When to choose Nextcloud: Nextcloud is ideal for larger teams, enterprises, or organizations that require high scalability, flexibility, and control over their data. It's suitable for teams with technical expertise and resources to set up and maintain a self-hosted solution, and those who prioritize data ownership and security.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox data using the Dropbox API or a third-party tool, such as Duplicati or rclone.
2. Set up your Nextcloud instance, either on a self-hosted server or through a managed provider.
3. Import your exported data into Nextcloud using the built-in import tool or a third-party migration script.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as user accounts and permissions, to complete the migration.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a robust and feature-rich platform for cloud storage and collaboration. However, one specific technical limitation worth noting is the requirement for technical expertise to set up and maintain a self-hosted instance, which can be a barrier for smaller teams or individuals. We recommend switching to Nextcloud for teams that prioritize data ownership, security, and scalability, while individuals or small teams who value ease of use and don't require advanced customization may want to stick with Dropbox.

## Who Should Switch
* Large enterprises with over 100 users who require high scalability and customization
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and security, such as financial or healthcare organizations
* Developers or tech-savvy individuals who can handle self-hosting and customization
* Organizations with existing infrastructure and resources to support self-hosting
* Teams that don't require advanced third-party integrations or ease of use

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud with my existing Dropbox account?
No, you will need to create a new account and migrate your data to use Nextcloud. 
### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting, but you will need to cover server costs.
### Can I integrate Nextcloud with other tools and services?
Yes, Nextcloud has a range of integrations with third-party tools and services, including onlyOffice and Collabora Online.
### Is Nextcloud suitable for small teams or individuals?
Not necessarily, as Nextcloud requires technical expertise to set up and maintain, which can be a barrier for smaller teams or individuals.
### Can I migrate my Dropbox data to Nextcloud directly?
Not directly, you will need to use a third-party tool or the Dropbox API to export your data before importing it into Nextcloud.

- **Self-hosting**: Jitsi deploys on a small VPS in minutes; Zoom cannot be self-hosted

### How hard is it to migrate from Zoom to Jitsi Meet?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Zoom data, follow the Jitsi Meet import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Jitsi Meet get regular updates?
Yes. Jitsi Meet has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

# Asana vs Taiga (2026)

## Overview
Asana and Taiga are project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Asana to Taiga, particularly those seeking more control over their data and a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration and task management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and autonomy over their project management platform.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Asana offers a free plan with limited features, while Taiga is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Taiga allows users to self-host and maintain full control over their data, whereas Asana stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Asana has a more straightforward setup process, while Taiga requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Taiga is highly scalable, especially for self-hosted instances, while Asana's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration difference: Taiga has native integration with Git repositories, while Asana relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

| Aspect | Asana | Taiga |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10.99+/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |

**Asana:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Robust feature set for team collaboration
* Integrates with many third-party tools

**Taiga:**

On the other hand, Taiga is perfect for teams that value data ownership, scalability, and customization. # Microsoft Teams vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Microsoft Teams and Mattermost are two popular team collaboration platforms that offer a range of features to enhance communication and productivity. Both tools are designed for teams and organizations looking to streamline their workflow and improve collaboration. * Data ownership: Mattermost allows users to self-host their instance, giving them full control over their data, whereas Microsoft Teams stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Microsoft Teams is generally easier to set up and requires less technical expertise, while Mattermost requires more technical knowledge to self-host.
* Scalability: Microsoft Teams is designed to scale with large enterprises, while Mattermost is also scalable but may require more configuration.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, allowing for seamless project management and tracking, whereas Microsoft Teams requires a third-party connector.

| Aspect | Microsoft Teams | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $6-$22/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $300-$1,100/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,200-$4,400/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Microsoft Teams:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Integrates well with other Microsoft tools
* Offers a free version
* Scalable and reliable
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Mattermost:**
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible
* Free and open-source
* Scalable and reliable
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup
